summary.text: A finite base analysis and an inductive study of the boundary run patterns give exact recurrences \(\ell_{n+1}=\ell_n+r_n\), \(r_{n+1}+1=r_n+q_n\), and \(q_{n+1}=q_n+\ell_{n-4}\) for the lengths of a reversed row and its first two run-length transforms. Choosing \(L\in[3/2,8/5]\) with \(L^4(L-1)^3=1\), these recurrences yield constant-factor bounds \(L^n/16\le a_n\le20L^n\), so taking \(n\)-th roots and squeezing proves convergence to \(L\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(X)\) denote the list of lengths of the maximal constant runs in a finite list \(X\). We write concatenation by juxtaposition or by \(\mathbin{\|}\), reversal as \(X^{\rm rev}\), and use \(\operatorname{tail}X\) and \(\operatorname{dropLast}X\) in their usual senses.

Let \(T_n\) be the rows of A381587, indexed from 1, so that
\[
T_1=[1],\qquad T_2=[1],\qquad T_3=[2],
\]
and, for \(n\geq 3\),
\[
T_{n+1}=D(T_n^{\rm rev})\mathbin{\|}T_n.
\]
The sequence in the question is
\[
a_n=\sum T_n.
\]
We prove that \(a_n^{1/n}\) has a limit. In fact, the proof identifies the limit as the real number \(L\in[3/2,8/5]\) satisfying
\[
L^4(L-1)^3=1.
\]
Numerically, this number is approximately \(1.55505757662408\).

We first record the elementary facts about run-length encoding that will be used below.

1. Every entry of \(D(X)\) is positive, and if \(X\neq[]\), then \(D(X)\neq[]\).

2. The runs partition the entries of \(X\), hence
\[
\sum D(X)=|X|.
\]

3. Reversal reverses the order of the runs but does not alter their lengths:
\[
D(X^{\rm rev})=D(X)^{\rm rev}.
\]

4. If \(a\neq b\), the boundary between \(a\) and \(b\) separates two runs. Thus, for arbitrary lists \(X,Y\),
\[
D(X\mathbin{\|}[a,b]\mathbin{\|}Y)
 =D(X\mathbin{\|}[a])\mathbin{\|}D([b]\mathbin{\|}Y).
\tag{1}
\]

5. Removing the final element of a list changes only its final run. More precisely, if
\[
D(X)=Z\mathbin{\|}[1],
\]
then
\[
D(\operatorname{dropLast}X)=Z,
\tag{2}
\]
and if
\[
D(X)=Z\mathbin{\|}[j+2],
\]
then
\[
D(\operatorname{dropLast}X)=Z\mathbin{\|}[j+1].
\tag{3}
\]

For completeness, these facts follow directly by decomposing a nonempty list into its first maximal run and the remaining list. If the first run consists of \(k+1\) copies of \(a\), then its contribution to \(D\) is \(k+1\); if a following entry exists, it differs from \(a\), so the encoding continues independently after that boundary. This proves (1) and the sum identity by induction. Applying the same maximal-run decomposition from the opposite end proves the reversal identity. Finally, (2) and (3) simply say that deleting the last list entry deletes a final run of length 1, or decreases a longer final run by 1.

It is convenient to reverse every row. Put
\[
W_n=T_n^{\rm rev}.
\]
Reversing the row recurrence and using the reversal identity for \(D\) gives, for every \(n\geq3\),
\[
W_{n+1}=W_n\mathbin{\|}D(W_n)^{\rm rev}.
\tag{4}
\]

We shall need a structural invariant for these lists. First note a simpler persistent shape. For every \(n\geq6\), there are lists \(t,z,w\) such that
\[
W_n=[2,1,1,1,3,1]\mathbin{\|}t,
\tag{5}
\]
\[
W_n=[2,1]\mathbin{\|}z\mathbin{\|}[3,1],
\tag{6}
\]
and
\[
W_n=w\mathbin{\|}[3,1].
\tag{7}
\]
Indeed, direct calculation gives
\[
W_6=[2,1,1,1,3,1].
\]
If (5) holds, then its initial pattern shows
\[
D(W_n)=[1,3,1,3]\mathbin{\|}D([3,1]\mathbin{\|}t)

\]
with the evident interpretation of the continuation; in particular \(D(W_n)\) starts with \([1,3]\). Therefore \(D(W_n)^{\rm rev}\) ends with \([3,1]\). Equation (4) retains the whole old \(W_n\) as a prefix and appends a list ending in \([3,1]\). Thus (5), (6), and (7) all persist. This proves the claim by induction.

We next establish the more detailed eventual invariant that produces the length recurrences. Define
\[
R_n=D(W_n),\qquad Q_n=D(R_n),\qquad V_n=D(Q_n),
\]
and let
\[
P=[1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,5,1,1,1].
\]
We claim that for every \(m\geq11\):

(i) there is a list \(R''\) such that
\[
R_m=R''\mathbin{\|}[5,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,1];
\tag{8}
\]

(ii) there is a list \(t\) such that
\[
Q_m=P\mathbin{\|}t\mathbin{\|}[1,6];
\tag{9}
\]

(iii)
\[
V_m=[6]\mathbin{\|}\operatorname{tail}(W_{m-4}).
\tag{10}
\]

Here is the finite base calculation at \(m=11\). Iterating (4) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_{11}={}&[2,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,3,1,\\
&1,1,1,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,7,1,1,1,1,1,\\
&5,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,3,1].
\end{aligned}
\]
Its successive run-length encodings are
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{11}={}&[1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,1,1,7,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,7,1,1,1,\\
&5,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,1],\\
Q_{11}={}&[1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,5,1,1,1,5,1,3,1,1,1,6],\\
V_{11}={}&[6,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus (8) holds with
\[
R''=[1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,1,1,7,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,7,1,1,1],
\]
and (9) holds with \(t=[5,1,3,1,1]\). Also
\[
W_7=[2,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1],
\]
so \(V_{11}=[6]\mathbin{\|}\operatorname{tail}(W_7)\), proving (10).

We now prove that the invariant propagates. Fix \(m\geq11\) and assume (8)–(10). For readability write
\[
R=R_m,\qquad Q=Q_m,\qquad V=V_m.
\]
By (7), write
\[
W_m=w\mathbin{\|}[3,1].
\tag{11}
\]
By (6), applied to \(m-4\), write
\[
W_{m-4}=[2,1]\mathbin{\|}z\mathbin{\|}[3,1].
\tag{12}
\]
Equation (4) says
\[
W_{m+1}=W_m\mathbin{\|}R^{\rm rev}.
\tag{13}
\]

We spell out the boundary calculations, since this is the combinatorial core of the proof. From (11), the last two entries of \(W_m\) are distinct, so (1) gives
\[
R=D(w\mathbin{\|}[3])\mathbin{\|}[1],
\qquad
\operatorname{dropLast}R=D(w\mathbin{\|}[3]).
\tag{14}
\]
From (8),
\[
R^{\rm rev}=[1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,5]\mathbin{\|}(R'')^{\rm rev}.
\tag{15}
\]
Taking the run lengths of (15), and using reversal, shows
\[
Q^{\rm rev}=[6]\mathbin{\|}D([3,1,5]\mathbin{\|}(R'')^{\rm rev}).
\]
Consequently
\[
(\operatorname{dropLast}Q)^{\rm rev}
 =D([3,1,5]\mathbin{\|}(R'')^{\rm rev}).
\tag{16}
\]
Substitute (11) and (15) into (13). At the join, the final 1 of \(W_m\) meets six initial 1's from \(R^{\rm rev}\), producing one run of length 7. All other runs are separated as in (14) and (16). Therefore
\[
R_{m+1}=
(\operatorname{dropLast}R)\mathbin{\|}[7]\mathbin{\|}
(\operatorname{dropLast}Q)^{\rm rev}.
\tag{17}
\]

Next, (8) and (9) imply
\[
\operatorname{dropLast}R=R''\mathbin{\|}[5,1,3,1,1,1,1,1],
\tag{18}
\]
\[
\operatorname{dropLast}Q=P\mathbin{\|}t\mathbin{\|}[1].
\tag{19}
\]
Because \(D(R)=Q\) ends in 6, deleting the last entry of \(R\) shortens that last run from 6 to 5. By (3),
\[
D(\operatorname{dropLast}R)
=(\operatorname{dropLast}Q)\mathbin{\|}[5].
\tag{20}
\]
On the other hand, (10) and (12) give
\[
V=[6,1]\mathbin{\|}z\mathbin{\|}[3,1],
\tag{21}
\]
and hence
\[
V^{\rm rev}=[1,3]\mathbin{\|}z^{\rm rev}\mathbin{\|}[1,6].
\tag{22}
\]
Since \(D(Q)=V\) ends in 1, (2) gives
\[
D(\operatorname{dropLast}Q)=[6,1]\mathbin{\|}z\mathbin{\|}[3].
\tag{23}
\]
Now apply \(D\) to (17). The boundary between the last 1 displayed in (18) and the inserted 7 is a genuine run boundary, as is the boundary from 7 to the first entry of the reversed part. Using (19), (20), (22), (23), and reversal of run encodings, one obtains
\[
Q_{m+1}=
(\operatorname{dropLast}Q)\mathbin{\|}[5]\mathbin{\|}V^{\rm rev}.
\tag{24}
\]
This identity also shows directly that \(Q_{m+1}\) again has the form (9): using (19) and (22), one may take the new middle list to be
\[
t\mathbin{\|}[1,5,1,3]\mathbin{\|}z^{\rm rev}.
\]
Likewise, (17) and (19) show that \(R_{m+1}\) has the suffix required in (8); explicitly, one may take its new initial part to be
\[
(\operatorname{dropLast}R)\mathbin{\|}[7,1]\mathbin{\|}t^{\rm rev}
 \mathbin{\|}[1,1,1].
\]

It remains to check (10) at \(m+1\). From (21), (12), and elementary run encoding,
\[
D(V)=D(W_{m-4}).
\tag{25}
\]
Indeed, in both lists the initial unequal pair is followed by the same \(z\mathbin{\|}[3,1]\), and replacing the first entry 2 by 6 does not change any equality or inequality between adjacent entries. By (4),
\[
W_{m-3}=W_{m-4}\mathbin{\|}D(W_{m-4})^{\rm rev}.
\tag{26}
\]
Finally apply \(D\) to (24). Using the explicit fixed prefix \(P\), the displayed forms (19) and (22), the unequal boundary \(1\neq5\), equations (23), (25), and reversal, the initial six equal 1's in \(P\) produce the first entry 6, while the remainder is exactly the tail of the concatenation in (26). Thus
\[
V_{m+1}=[6]\mathbin{\|}\operatorname{tail}(W_{m-3})
=[6]\mathbin{\|}\operatorname{tail}(W_{m+1-4}).
\tag{27}
\]
This is (10) for \(m+1\). The induction is complete, so (8)–(10), together with (17) and (24), hold for every \(m\geq11\).

We now pass from lists to lengths. Define
\[
\ell_n=|W_n|,\qquad r_n=|D(W_n)|=|R_n|,
\qquad q_n=|D(D(W_n))|=|Q_n|.
\]
The rows \(W_n\) are nonempty for \(n\geq1\), and therefore so are all their iterated run encodings.

Taking lengths in (4) gives, for \(n\geq3\),
\[
\ell_{n+1}=\ell_n+r_n.
\tag{28}
\]
For \(n\geq11\), take lengths in (17). Removing the final entry decreases the length by 1, reversal preserves length, and the inserted \([7]\) contributes 1. Hence
\[
r_{n+1}=(r_n-1)+1+(q_n-1)=r_n+q_n-1,
\]
or equivalently
\[
r_{n+1}+1=r_n+q_n.
\tag{29}
\]
Similarly, (24) gives
\[
q_{n+1}=(q_n-1)+1+|V_n|.
\]
By (10), \(|V_n|=1+|\operatorname{tail}(W_{n-4})|=\ell_{n-4}\), since \(W_{n-4}\neq[]\). Therefore
\[
q_{n+1}=q_n+\ell_{n-4}.
\tag{30}
\]
If we put \(z_n=q_n-1\), equations (28)–(30) become the particularly transparent system
\[
\boxed{
\ell_{n+1}=\ell_n+r_n,
\qquad r_{n+1}=r_n+z_n,
\qquad z_{n+1}=z_n+\ell_{n-4}
}
\tag{31}
\]
for \(n\geq11\).

We next choose the exponential rate. The continuous function
\[
f(x)=x^4(x-1)^3
\]
satisfies
\[
f(3/2)=\frac{81}{128}<1,
\qquad
f(8/5)=\frac{110592}{78125}>1.
\]
The intermediate value theorem therefore supplies an \(L\in[3/2,8/5]\) such that
\[
L^4(L-1)^3=1.
\tag{32}
\]
In particular, \(L>0\).

The reason for equation (32) is now visible. The three sequences
\[
L^n,\qquad L^n(L-1),\qquad L^n(L-1)^2
\tag{33}
\]
satisfy exactly the homogeneous comparison version of (31). The first two identities follow from \(1+(L-1)=L\). For the third,
\[
L^n(L-1)^2+L^{n-4}
 =L^{n+1}(L-1)^2,
\tag{34}
\]
because the difference between the right side and the first term on the left is
\(L^n(L-1)^3=L^{n-4}\), by (32).

We use (33) to bound the actual integer sequences. We claim that for all \(n\geq11\),
\[
\frac1{10}L^n\leq \ell_n\leq10L^n,
\tag{35}
\]
\[
\frac1{10}L^n(L-1)\leq r_n\leq10L^n(L-1),
\tag{36}
\]
and
\[
\frac1{10}L^n(L-1)^2\leq q_n-1\leq10L^n(L-1)^2.
\tag{37}
\]

The required initial values, obtained by iterating the displayed row recurrence and counting runs, are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
n&11&12&13&14&15\\ \hline
\ell_n&66&102&156&238&364\\
r_n&36&54&82&126&196\\
q_n&19&29&45&71&113.
\end{array}
\tag{38}
\]
These values give (35)–(37) for \(11\leq n\leq15\). Here is a convenient way to check the inequalities without knowing the exact value of \(L\). Since
\[
\frac32\leq L\leq\frac85,
\qquad
\frac12\leq L-1\leq\frac35,
\qquad
\frac14\leq(L-1)^2\leq\frac9{25},
\]
the lower bounds follow from the stronger comparisons
\[
\frac1{10}\left(\frac85\right)^n\leq\ell_n,
\quad
\frac1{10}\left(\frac85\right)^n\frac35\leq r_n,
\quad
\frac1{10}\left(\frac85\right)^n\frac9{25}\leq q_n-1,
\]
and the upper bounds follow from
\[
\ell_n\leq10\left(\frac32\right)^n,
\quad
r_n\leq10\left(\frac32\right)^n\frac12,
\quad
q_n-1\leq10\left(\frac32\right)^n\frac14.
\]
Substitution of the five columns of (38) verifies these elementary rational inequalities.

For the induction step, suppose \(n\geq15\) and the bounds are known at all earlier needed indices. Equations (31) express each new quantity as the sum of two old quantities. Adding the two lower bounds in (35) and (36), and using the first model identity in (33), gives the lower bound for \(\ell_{n+1}\); adding the corresponding upper bounds gives its upper bound. The same argument with (36) and (37) gives the bounds for \(r_{n+1}\). Finally, add the bounds for \(q_n-1\) and \(\ell_{n-4}\); identity (34) gives exactly the desired bounds for \(q_{n+1}-1\). Thus (35)–(37) hold for every \(n\geq11\).

We finally return to the row sums. Since reversal does not alter length, and since the sum of a run-length encoding is the length of the encoded list, the row recurrence gives, for \(n\geq3\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+1}
 &=\sum D(W_n)+\sum T_n\\
 &=|W_n|+a_n\\
 &=\ell_n+a_n.
\end{aligned}
\tag{39}
\]
A direct calculation gives \(a_{12}=175\).

We derive two-sided exponential bounds for \(a_n\). First, for every \(n\geq12\),
\[
a_n\leq20L^n.
\tag{40}
\]
At \(n=12\), this follows from \(a_{12}=175\) and \(L\geq3/2\). If it holds at \(n\), then by (39) and (35),
\[
a_{n+1}\leq20L^n+10L^n=30L^n
 \leq20L^{n+1},
\]
because \(L\geq3/2\).

For the lower bound, if \(n=k+1\geq12\), then (39), nonnegativity of \(a_k\), and (35) give
\[
a_n=a_k+\ell_k\geq\frac1{10}L^k.
\]
Since \(L\leq8/5\), we have \(L/16\leq1/10\), so
\[
a_n\geq\frac1{16}L^{k+1}=\frac1{16}L^n.
\tag{41}
\]
Combining (40) and (41), for every \(n\geq12\),
\[
\frac1{16}\leq \frac{a_n}{L^n}\leq20.
\tag{42}
\]
All quantities here are positive. Taking positive real \(n\)-th roots yields
\[
\left(\frac1{16}\right)^{1/n}
\leq
\left(\frac{a_n}{L^n}\right)^{1/n}
\leq
20^{1/n}.
\]
Both outer expressions tend to 1, since for every fixed \(c>0\), \(c^{1/n}\to1\). Hence, by the squeeze theorem,
\[
\left(\frac{a_n}{L^n}\right)^{1/n}\longrightarrow1.
\]
Because \(L>0\),
\[
a_n^{1/n}
 =L\left(\frac{a_n}{L^n}\right)^{1/n},
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n^{1/n}=L},
\]
where \(L\in[3/2,8/5]\) satisfies \(L^4(L-1)^3=1\). In particular, the requested limit exists.
